edges.effect_quant: Breastfeeding is one of the more consistent early-life protective exposures linked to lower later inflammatory bowel disease risk, and longer duration appears to strengthen the association.
edges.mechanism: Human milk shapes gut microbial colonization, intestinal barrier maturation, and mucosal immune signaling during a critical developmental window. That makes a later association with Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis biologically coherent, especially when protection strengthens with longer breastfeeding duration.
edges.summary: Compared with several other early-life hypotheses, this one holds up reasonably well. Meta-analyses consistently find lower later risk of inflammatory bowel disease among people who were breastfed in infancy, with the strongest reductions reported in longer-duration breastfeeding categories.
edges.caveats: The evidence is observational and combines studies across eras and regions with different formula practices and diagnostic standards. Even so, the direction of effect has been fairly stable across successive reviews.

evidence.citation: Klement E et al 2004 Am J Clin Nutr
evidence.notes: Breastfeeding and risk of inflammatory bowel disease: a systematic review with meta-analysis.
